exp.0:0:
Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, a messenger sent with authority from Christ. He says he is one "by the will of God": he did not choose this role for himself, he was called. He also mentions Timothy, whom he calls "our brother," a fellow worker and companion in faith.

This is the opening of a letter to the Christians of Colossae, a city in Asia Minor. Paul writes from prison. According to the text, he did not personally found that church; he probably came to know it through co-workers such as Epaphras. He includes Timothy as a companion, though that does not mean the two of them wrote the words. Many understand the voice to be Paul's.

For today: your life and your service have meaning when you remember that God called you. Serve with humility, knowing that other brothers and sisters walk alongside you and that you are not alone.
exp.0:2:
Paul says that he and Timothy give thanks to God, whom he calls "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." They do this whenever they pray for the Colossians. The word "you" in the verse refers to the people he is writing to. The word "always" shows that their thankfulness and their prayer were constant.

Paul writes this letter to a church in Colossae, a city that, according to the text, he had not visited in person; he had heard about them from others. He begins, as in his other letters, with thanksgiving before he teaches or corrects. The verses that follow explain the reason: he had heard of their faith, of their love for fellow believers, and of their hope in heaven.

For today: when you pray for other people, begin by giving thanks for the good that God is already doing in their lives. This changes your outlook, encourages others, and helps you pray with more love and less complaint.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the Colossians learned the gospel through Epaphras. Paul calls him our dear fellowservant, meaning a companion who serves the same Lord. He also describes him as a faithful minister of Christ, that is, a trustworthy servant who works on your behalf, for your benefit.

Paul writes this letter from prison, together with Timothy. He does not appear to have visited Colosse personally. For that reason he backs Epaphras: he wants the believers to know that what they received is the truth. According to the context, Epaphras also reported to Paul about their love. Scholars believe Epaphras founded or helped establish that church, although the letter does not give the details.

For today: give thanks for those who taught you the faith faithfully, and express your appreciation to them. And if you serve others, do so with steadiness, without seeking applause.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that, since the day he heard about the love and faith of the Colossians, he has not stopped praying for them. He asks that God would fill them with the knowledge of his will, with wisdom and spiritual understanding. The word "you" in the verse above refers to the Colossian believers themselves, and "understanding" here means insight that grasps what God is doing.

Paul writes from prison, together with Timothy, to a church he had never met in person. Epaphras, who taught them the gospel, told him how they were living. Paul responds with thanksgiving and prayer. His desire, according to the verses that follow, is that they would live in a way that pleases the Lord.

For today: knowing God's will is not only a matter of knowing facts, but of learning to live as He wants. You can pray this way for your family, your church, and your friends: not only for their problems, but that God would give them wisdom and understanding to obey Him each day.
exp.0:9:
Verse 10 says that Paul prays the believers will live in a way that honors the Lord. The phrase about walking worthy means living in a way that honors him. Pleasing him in everything means seeking to please him in every area of life. Being fruitful means producing good works, that is, doing good things. And growing in the knowledge of God means coming to know him better and better.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae, and together with Timothy he tells them that they do not stop praying for them. He was glad to hear of their love through Epaphras. His prayer asks that they understand God's will, and that this understanding be seen in a daily life that pleases him.

For today: knowing God is not only knowing facts, but it changes what we do. This week, think of one concrete act of kindness, such as helping someone or forgiving, and do it as something you offer to the Lord.
exp.0:10:
He says that God strengthens believers with every kind of strength, and that this strength comes from his glorious power. The purpose is that they may have endurance and patience, with bearing with others and with trials, and that they do it with joy.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae and tells them that he prays for them continually. Earlier he asked that they know God's will and live in a manner worthy of him. Now he adds that they need strength from God to live this way. Then he gratefully reminds them of what God has already done for them.

For today: when you lack patience with someone or with a difficult situation, do not rely only on your own effort. Ask God for his strength, and ask him also for joy while you wait.
exp.0:13:
In whom we have redemption, the explanation says, referring to Jesus, the beloved Son of the previous verse. This word speaks of being rescued by the payment of a price, like someone who sets a slave free. That price was his blood, that is, his death as a sacrifice. The result is the forgiveness of sins, which means pardon: our guilt no longer condemns us.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae from prison. He reminds them of what God has already done for them: he rescued them from the power of darkness and brought them into the kingdom of Christ. This forgiveness is the basis of that deliverance. Then Paul presents the greatness of Christ, so that no one adds other things to his work.

For today: when the guilt of the past weighs on you, remember that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts, but on what Christ did. Rest in that and live grateful.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that Jesus is the head of the church, which is his body. He is the beginning, and the first to rise from the dead, never to die again, opening the way for others. "Preeminence" means the first place, the one who is above all.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Colossae. Earlier he has shown that Christ created all things and holds them together. Later he will say that through his cross he reconciles all things to God. Paul wants them not to put anyone or anything above Christ.

For today: check what holds first place in your life. Each day, before deciding something, ask yourself how you can honor Christ in it. And remember that you do not follow Jesus alone, but united to his church.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that God the Father was pleased, freely and gladly, for all his fullness to dwell in Christ. The word "pleased" means it was his good will. "Fullness" means that everything God is and everything God wants to give is complete in Jesus. Nothing is lacking. Some scholars think it refers to the fullness of the divine nature, and others to the fullness of God's work and presence; both ideas fit with the rest of the letter.

Paul writes to the believers in Colossae to strengthen them in who Christ is. Earlier he speaks of Jesus as Creator, head of the church, and firstborn from the dead. Then he explains that, through his cross, God reconciles to himself those who were far away. Paul wants them not to seek other teachings that would add anything to Christ.

For today: if all the fullness of God dwells in Jesus, you do not need to look somewhere else for what you lack. Bring him your emptiness, your fears, and your questions today, with confidence.
exp.0:19:
It says that God wanted to reconcile all things to himself through Christ. That peace was achieved through the blood of his cross, that is, through his sacrificial death. The reach of this reconciliation covers what is on the earth and in the heavens.

Paul writes to the Christians in Colossae to show them that Jesus is supreme and sufficient. Earlier he speaks of Christ as the head of the church and the firstborn from the dead. Then he reminds them that they themselves were once enemies and are now reconciled. How this reconciliation applies to the things in the heavens is interpreted in several ways, and the text does not explain it in detail.

If you are far from God or carry guilt, the cross is the basis of peace with him. You do not need to earn it through effort; you can draw near by trusting in what Christ has already done.
exp.0:24:
Paul says that the church is the body of Christ and that he was made a minister, that is, a servant of it. God entrusted him with a task for the good of the Colossians. His mission is to fulfill the word of God, that is, to proclaim it in full, leaving nothing half done.

Paul writes from prison to a church he did not found. He wants to encourage them to remain firm in the gospel and not to be deceived by false teachings. He makes clear that his service was not his own idea but a charge from God, and that even his sufferings have meaning for their good. Afterward he will explain the mystery: Christ in them, the hope of glory.

For today: God gives each believer a concrete service. Ask him what he has entrusted to you, whether in your family, your work, or your church, and do it with faithfulness and joy.
exp.0:26:
This verse says that God chose to make known the precious and glorious nature of a secret that had been hidden before. A "mystery" here is not something strange, but a truth that God kept and later revealed. The explanation's word for "known" means made widely known, and "Gentiles" are the peoples who were not Jews. That secret is that Christ lives in you, and this gives the assurance that you will share in his glory.

The apostle Paul speaks here, writing to the believers in Colossae from prison. He explains that God entrusted him with the task of announcing this message. The important point is that salvation was no longer only for Israel, but also for the peoples of other nations. Paul wants them to grow strong and steady in Christ.

For today: when you feel far from God or not enough, remember that Christ is not far away but with you. Set aside a moment each day to speak with him and trust in his presence, because there is your hope.
exp.0:28:
Paul says that he labors and struggles with all his strength, yet he does not depend on himself. The idea of struggling, as an athlete strives, is rendered by the word "striving" in the verse, and the power at work is the power of Christ working strongly within Paul.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to the believers in Colossae. In the verses before, he explains his mission: to proclaim Christ, to counsel and teach everyone, so that each person grows and matures in Him. Here he makes clear that his effort is real, but the strength comes from Christ.

For today: when you serve others, your family, or the church, do your part with dedication, but do not lean only on your own strength. Ask God each day for His power to work in you, and rest in the knowledge that He sustains your labor.
exp.1:4:
Paul says that, although he is not physically present, his spirit is with the Colossians. He rejoices as he sees their order and good organization among them, and the steadfastness of their faith in Christ.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and he did not personally know the church in Colossae. He warned them against those who wanted to deceive them with persuasive words. Before correcting them, he encourages them: he acknowledges the good that is in them. He speaks like a pastor who cares for them from a distance, and we do not know in detail how he received the news, though it was probably through messengers.

For today: distance does not prevent us from caring for others. You can pray for, write to, or call someone who is far away. And before pointing out mistakes, learn to recognize and be thankful for what is good in the faith of others.
exp.1:5:
The explanation says that, just as the Colossians received Jesus Christ as Lord, they must keep living in him. The word "walk" means conducting one's life day by day, and "in him" means in union with Christ and depending on him. In other words, the Christian life continues the same way it began: by trusting in Jesus.

Paul writes from a distance, probably as a prisoner, to a church he himself had never visited. He is concerned about persuasive arguments and philosophies that could draw them away from Christ. For this reason he reminds them of what they had already received and asks them not to seek anything different or additional.

For today: if you began to follow Jesus through faith and gratitude, do not exchange that path for pressure, habit, or novelty. Each day, return to him through prayer, Bible reading, and simple obedience.
exp.1:7:
This verse warns us to be careful that no one takes us captive with ideas that sound clever but are empty. Arguments that are very clever and elaborate are the kind of thing it has in view. The phrase about the basic principles of this world can refer to the foundational patterns of this world, and some also understand it as spiritual forces; it is interpreted in several ways. The key point is that these ideas come from human traditions and not from Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Colossae from prison. He had told them to keep walking in Christ, firm in the faith. Now he protects them from teachings that wanted to add other things to Christ. Afterward he reminds them that in Christ dwells all the fullness of God.

For today: when you hear a new idea, whether it is fashionable, from social media, or even religious, ask yourself: "Does this draw me closer to Christ and agree with what He taught?" Read the Bible regularly so you can recognize what is true.
exp.1:11:
It says that when we are baptized, we are united with Christ in his death, as if we were buried with him. We are also united with his resurrection, as if we rose with him. This happens through faith in the power of God, who raised Jesus from the dead.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, who were receiving teachings that mixed Christ with human rituals and traditions. Earlier he had spoken of a spiritual cleansing done by God and not by human hands. Here he uses baptism as a picture of that new life. Some debate how much the rite itself is emphasized and how much the faith it represents, but the text stresses that the work belongs to God.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor through religious effort. Rest in what Christ has already done, and walk each day as someone who has new life, trusting in the power of God.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the foods, the festivals, the new moons, and the Sabbaths mentioned earlier were like a shadow, an outline that announced something that was going to come. The word "body" here means the reality itself, the true thing. That reality is Christ. The shadow points; Christ is the one who casts it.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, who were under pressure from teachers who demanded rules about food, special days, and a certain spirituality involving angels. Paul reminds them that Christ has already overcome every opposing power. Because of this, no one should judge them for those practices. Scholars debate exactly what that teaching was, but the central point is clear: Christ is sufficient.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are giving more weight to rules or customs than to Christ himself. Traditions can help, but they must not take his place. Let us seek first to know him.
exp.1:18:
The explanation says that there are people who are not united to Christ, the head. The phrase about ligaments and joints is like the muscles and joints that connect the body. The word about being nourished and knit together means being well fed and firmly joined together. In this way, the church grows with the growth that God gives, when it is connected to Christ.

Paul writes to the Colossians from prison to warn them against teachers who wanted to disqualify them with rules, visions, and the worship of angels. These teachers considered themselves very spiritual, but they were proud. Paul reminds them that everything they need is found in Christ, not in added practices. Scholars disagree about exactly who these teachers were.

Today: do not seek to grow spiritually only through rules or impressive experiences. Stay close to Christ through his Word, prayer, and fellowship with other believers, because God makes his church grow when we are united to him and to one another.
exp.2:1:
Paul asks us to set our minds, that is, our thoughts, interest, and affection, on the things above, and not on the things on the earth.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, very likely from prison. He reminds them that, through faith, they have been raised with Christ, who is seated at the right hand of God. Because of this, their way of thinking must change. The things of the earth are not evil in themselves, but they should not be what matters most. Their true life is secure in Christ.

Today you can begin the day with a short pause: ask God to guide your priorities. When worries, money, or pressures come up, ask yourself: "How can I act today in a way that honors Christ?"
exp.2:3:
This verse says that Christ is our life. Today that life is hidden, but when Jesus is revealed openly (that is, when he returns), believers will also be revealed with him, sharing in his glory. The word "you" in this verse is the same "you" we use today.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae. He reminds them that, by being joined to Christ, they died to their old way of living, and now their true identity is in him. This future hope serves as the foundation for what follows: leaving behind the sins that harm the new life.

For today: when you feel undervalued or tired of struggling, remember that your real life is secure in Christ, even though it is not yet visible. That hope encourages you to say no to sin and to live today in a way that reflects his glory.
exp.2:5:
The explanation says that God does not look with indifference on the wrongs mentioned before: sexual immorality, impurity, disordered passions, and greed. Because of these things, his wrath comes, that is, his righteous opposition to evil, on the children of disobedience, meaning those who live in disobedience and resist God. Some early manuscripts leave out the phrase about the children of disobedience, but the overall meaning does not change.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Colossae. He reminds them that, being united with Christ, they already have a new life. For this reason he asks them to leave behind the behavior of their former life. The warning about God's wrath shows them how serious that path is.

For today: honestly examine which habit or desire you are still justifying. Bring it before God, ask him for help, and take one concrete step to leave it, remembering that Christ gives you a new life.
exp.2:20:
The explanation says that fathers should not provoke their children or treat them in a way that makes them angry or upset without reason. The reason is that children can become discouraged, lose confidence, and lose the will to keep going. The word "provoke" in the verse means to stir up anger, and the verse's word "discouraged" means to be disheartened or without strength.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colosse. In this part he explains how faith is lived out at home. Earlier he asked children to obey; now he reminds parents that their authority must be exercised with care and love. Everyone in the family answers to the Lord.

For today: correct your children with firmness, but without shouting, mockery, or unfair demands. Listen, acknowledge their efforts, and encourage them. In this way, discipline helps them grow instead of wounding them.
exp.3:2:
Paul asks the Colossians to pray for him and his companions too. He wants God to open for them a door for the message, that is, an opportunity to proclaim the mystery of Christ: God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Jesus. Being in bonds means he was chained for preaching this.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, though some scholars have suggested another place. He has just asked them to pray with steadfastness and thankfulness. He does not ask to be released from prison, but that the message keep moving forward. His aim is to speak clearly, as the next verse says.

For today: when you pray for others, ask that God give them opportunities to speak of Christ, even in difficult circumstances. Pray for yourself as well: that God open doors for you and give you wisdom to share your faith with love and clarity.
exp.3:8:
Paul says that Tychicus will be accompanied by Onesimus, whom he calls a faithful and beloved brother, and he clarifies that Onesimus is one of you, that is, from the city of Colossae. Together the two of them will tell you everything that is happening where Paul is.

Paul writes this letter from prison. He wants the Colossians to know how he is doing and to be encouraged. Many understand that this Onesimus is the slave the letter to Philemon speaks of, but the text here does not say so, so it is not entirely certain. What we do see is that Paul receives him with great affection.

For today: God can use anyone, regardless of their past, as a faithful messenger. If someone arrives at your church with a difficult story, welcome them as a brother and give them the opportunity to serve.
exp.3:11:
Epaphras sends you his greetings. He is one of you, from your own city, and he is a servant of Christ. He always works hard for you in prayer, asking that you stand firm, mature, and fully assured in everything God desires. Epaphras is concerned, attentive, and devoted to you.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Colossae. Epaphras was from there, and according to chapter 1, he was probably the one who taught them the gospel. Paul mentions him to encourage them: someone far from them is carrying them in prayer with real effort. Laodicea and Hierapolis, nearby cities, are also mentioned.

For today: pray for someone in your church or family with steadiness and by name. Don't only ask that things go well for them, but that they stand firm and grow in the will of God.
exp.1:21:
Paul says that the things these rules deal with (foods, drinks, and things not to be touched) are used up and worn out by the very act of using them. They have no lasting value. Moreover, these rules do not come from God, but are based on "human commands and teachings." The phrase "perish with use" means that these things perish as they are used.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, who were being pressured by teachers who demanded strict rules, rituals, and harsh treatment of the body in order to be more spiritual. Paul reminds them that, being united to Christ, they have already died to the basic principles or elemental powers of the world. Therefore they should not submit to those human regulations.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are measuring our faith by external rules that someone invented, instead of trusting in what Christ has already done. Obedience is good, but it springs from a new life in Him, not from fear or outward appearance.
exp.3:14:
This verse asks the Colossians to greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea for Paul, along with Nympha and the church that meets at her house. The word translated "greet" means to send greetings to someone. In the verse you are reading, Nympha is a woman's name, although some ancient manuscripts read "Nymphas" as a masculine name, and it is not certain which is correct.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Colossae. Laodicea was a nearby city, and the two congregations had a close relationship. Paul ends the letter with personal greetings, which shows that he saw the churches as one family. The early Christians often met in homes.

For today: a large building is not needed to live out the faith in community. We can open our homes, or greet and encourage other believers, even when they are far away.
exp.2:13:
It says that, over all the other virtues mentioned before, we should clothe ourselves with love. In this translation, the word for love is the Greek word agape, which refers to a deep, committed kind of love, and the word translated as "bond" is a tie that joins things together. "Perfect unity" points to a community that is whole and working together. Love is what holds all the other virtues together.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae. He explains how a person lives who has been made new in Christ. Earlier he spoke of compassion, humility and forgiveness. Here love appears as the main garment that completes everything else and keeps the community united.

Today, before you react to someone who has upset you at home, at work or at church, ask yourself: "Am I acting with love?" Ask God for help to forgive and to treat that person well, even when it is hard.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that Christ stripped the powers and authorities opposed to God of their control. The word "disarmed" means he took away the weapons they relied on, and the phrase "made a public spectacle of them" means he displayed them defeated, like a victory parade. The reference to triumphing "by the cross" shows that Jesus won this victory through his death there.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, who were under pressure from teachings that mixed rituals, rules and fear of spiritual powers. Earlier, Paul explained that Christ canceled the debt of sin by nailing it to the cross. For this reason, no one should make them feel condemned over food or festivals, which were only a shadow; the reality is in Christ.

Today, if you feel fear or guilt, remember that Jesus has already triumphed on the cross. Rest in his forgiveness and trust in his authority, not in rituals or superstitions.
exp.3:5:
Paul says our speech should always be gracious and pleasant, but also seasoned with salt, meaning with flavor and substance, never bland or empty. Salt adds taste and also helps keep things wholesome, so some see in it a picture of words that are sound and full of truth. The goal is to know how to respond to everyone, giving each person the answer that fits their need.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Colossae. Just before this, he asked them to pray for him and told them to act wisely toward those outside the faith. Their manner of speaking was meant to reflect Christ and help others come to hear the good news.

For today: before you respond to someone, especially if they are upset or have doubts, pause briefly and ask God for help to answer with kindness and truth.
exp.0:16:
It says that Christ existed before anything that was created, and that everything holds together in him. The phrase "hold together" in the verse means that things keep existing, are held up, and remain bound together. He did not only create the universe; he also sustains it today.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Colossae, who were receiving teachings that made Jesus just one more among other spiritual beings. That is why Paul presents him as the Creator, superior to "thrones, dominions, principalities and powers." Then he says that Christ is also the head of the church.

For today: when you feel that your life or the world is falling apart, remember that Christ holds everything together. You can hand him your worries with confidence, because nothing slips out of his hands. Begin the day in prayer: "Lord, hold up what I cannot hold up."
exp.3:10:
This verse mentions a man named Jesus, who was also known as Justus. It was a common name at that time, so this is not the Lord Jesus. Paul says that he, along with Aristarchus and Mark, is a Jew, a believer of Jewish background. Of all the Jewish people around him, only these three were helping him in the work of God's kingdom, and Paul says they have been a comfort to him.

Paul writes this letter from prison and sends final greetings to the church in Colossae. Here he recognizes his closest co-workers. It is notable that, although he was Jewish, he valued equally companions from other backgrounds, such as Epaphras and Onesimus, who were not Jewish.

For today: value and thank those who stand by you faithfully, especially in difficult times. Tell someone that their support has been a comfort to you.
exp.0:27:
He says that Paul and his companions proclaim Christ. They do this by admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom. Their goal is to present everyone as mature in Christ. Here "mature" means grown, complete, or adult in faith, not without any mistakes.

Paul writes to the believers in Colossae from prison. The mystery is Christ, who is now also made known to people who are not Jewish. Paul explains why he works so hard: he wants everyone to grow up to maturity in Christ, not just to begin believing. Also, there were false teachings that threatened that church.

For today: help others grow in Christ with patience, truth, and love. Encourage, teach, and correct with humility, and remember that you too still need to keep growing.
exp.0:25:
It speaks of a "mystery," that is, something God had kept hidden and which people could not understand on their own. It was hidden "for ages and generations," meaning for a very long time. But now God has revealed it to "his saints," who are the believers, those who belong to God. The word "revealed" means made known clearly.

The passage is written by the apostle Paul, writing to the Colossians from prison. He explains that he serves the church by proclaiming the word of God. In the verses that follow he clarifies that this mystery is "Christ in you, the hope of glory," and that it is for all peoples, the non-Jews included.

Today we can be thankful that God did not stay distant or silent. If you know Christ, it is not because of your own cleverness, but because God chose to make himself known. This invites us to share that news with humility and joy.
exp.3:17:
Paul closes the letter by writing a few lines himself, in his own hand, as a personal signature. He asks them to remember his chains, that is, his imprisonment. He ends by wishing them the grace of God.

Paul used to dictate his letters to an assistant, and at the end he took up the pen to sign and give the letter its authority. He was in prison for preaching the gospel. His request is not a plea for pity, but for prayer and for remembrance of what it costs to proclaim Christ. The letter was carried to Colossae by Tychicus and Onesimus.

Today we can remember believers who suffer for their faith, pray for them, and support them. And we can end our conversations by wishing others the grace of God, not merely saying goodbye out of habit.
exp.2:2:
The verse says that believers "died," meaning their former way of living, separated from God, no longer has power over them. Now their true life is hidden, or kept safe, together with Christ in God, secure, even though the world cannot yet see it. The phrase "you died" is understood as a spiritual death to sin because of being united with Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae. He reminds them that, since they were raised with Christ, they should focus their minds on heavenly things. Later he asks them to put aside practices such as immorality and greed. Their new identity is the basis for that change in conduct.

For today: when you feel defined by your mistakes or by what others think, remember who you are in Christ. That security gives you strength to say no to what harms you and to seek what pleases God.
exp.2:7:
This verse says that believers must put aside certain behaviors. "Anger" and "rage" are the fury that is held inside and then bursts out. "Malice" is the desire to hurt someone. "Slander" is speaking badly about others, insulting them, or spreading lies about them. "Filthy language" is coarse or shameful speech.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Colossae. He reminds them that they used to live this way, just like those who rebel against God. Now, through their faith in Christ, they are called to a new life. He will later tell them to take off the old self and put on the new, the way someone changes clothes.

For today: this week, when you feel the urge to shout, criticize, or let out a hurtful word, pause and pray briefly. Then choose to respond with calm and respect, even when it is hard.
exp.2:11:
Paul tells the believers to "clothe yourselves," the way someone puts on new clothes, with certain qualities. He names a heart of compassion, which is a tender, caring attitude toward others; kindness, which is goodness shown in action; humility, which is not thinking oneself better than others; gentleness, which is treating people with a calm and non-violent spirit; and patience, which is the ability to bear with others over time. He grounds this by reminding them that they are chosen, holy, and loved by God.

Paul writes to the church in Colossae, probably from prison. He has just spoken about leaving the old life and putting on the new one in Christ, where differences of origin or social standing do not matter. That is why this clothing is for everyone alike, and he soon speaks of forgiving one another.

For today: before reacting to someone who bothers you, remember that God loves you and has forgiven you. Ask Him to help you respond with patience and kindness.
exp.3:9:
Paul sends greetings from Aristarchus, who is imprisoned with him, and from Mark, the cousin of Barnabas. The Greek word behind "cousin" most likely means a close relative of this kind, so this is the relationship the verse describes. Paul reminds the Colossians that they have already received instructions about Mark, and he asks them to welcome him if he comes to visit them.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the church in Colossae. Mark had left Paul and Barnabas on an earlier journey (Acts 13:13), and that caused tension between them (Acts 15:37-39). Now Paul mentions him with confidence. We do not know what instructions the Colossians received earlier, but Paul hopes that Mark will be welcomed warmly.

Today, this invites us to give second chances. If someone failed and has changed, let us welcome them without holding a grudge, and help others to accept them too.
exp.1:10:
He says that believers in Christ have received a spiritual circumcision, performed not by human hands. It consists of setting aside or leaving behind the sinful nature, which Paul calls "your sinful nature" in this wording. The phrase "in the putting off" means taking something off, like an old set of clothes. This work is done by Christ in the one who believes.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, who were being influenced by teachings that added Jewish rules and rituals as a requirement for being complete. Paul answers that in Christ they already have everything. Some understand "the circumcision performed by Christ" as referring to his death, and others as the inner work he does in the believer. The following text joins it with baptism and new life.

Today, you do not have to earn God's favor through religious effort. Trust in what Christ has already done, and let him transform your heart.
exp.2:4:
It says we should "put to death" the earthly parts of our nature, that is, make dead what belongs to our earthly life. Then it gives a list: sexual immorality, impurity, lust (indulging in pleasures without restraint), evil desires, and greed (always wanting more). Paul says that greed is idolatry because it puts things in the place of God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Colossae. He has just told them that they have already died with Christ and that their true life is hidden in God. For that reason he asks them to live in line with that new identity. Then he warns that God opposes these behaviors, and he reminds them that they themselves once lived this way.

For today: identify a desire or habit that dominates you, such as money, screens, or a hidden pleasure. Bring it before God in prayer and ask for his help to leave it behind, remembering that you already belong to Christ.
exp.0:1:
This verse is the greeting at the start of the letter. It is addressed to the "saints," meaning those whom God has set apart for himself, and to the "faithful brothers in Christ" who lived in Colossae. Paul wishes them "grace," which is God's favor given freely and not earned, and "peace," which is the calm and reconciliation with him.

Paul writes together with Timothy to a church in Colossae, a city in Asia Minor. From what the letter says, it does not seem that he had personally founded it. He writes to encourage them and strengthen them in their faith in Christ. His greeting names God our Father as the source of every blessing.

For today: we can begin each day by remembering that our identity comes from Christ, not from our achievements. If you are living anxiously, ask God for his peace and rest in his grace.
exp.3:12:
Paul says he can testify with certainty that Epaphras goes to great pains for the believers in Colosse, in Laodicea, and in Hierapolis. Here "great pains" means a deep concern and sincere devotion, a serious effort made for their good.

Paul writes from prison and is finishing his letter. Epaphras was from Colosse and had worked among these churches in the region. The previous verse says he always prayed for them. Paul wants the Colossians to know that this man truly cares for them and that his teaching deserves trust.

For today: pray consistently and by name for your church and for other communities nearby. Christian love does not stop at good intentions; it shows in the daily effort of interceding for others, even when no one sees it.
exp.0:14:
He says that Jesus is the image of the invisible God: in him we can see what God is like, even though no one can see God directly. "Firstborn" referred to the eldest son, who held special honor and authority. "Over all creation" means over everything that has been made. So Christ holds the first place over all of creation. Some Christians understand this as rank and supremacy, not as Jesus having been created, and the next verse supports that reading: through him all things were created.

Paul writes to the believers in Colossae. He has just spoken of redemption through the blood of Christ, and now he presents who the Savior is: not someone lesser, but God himself revealed, Lord of all. He wants to strengthen them in their faith against teachings that diminished Christ.

For today: if you want to know what God is like, look to Jesus. Read the Gospels and let his character correct your ideas about God.
exp.1:12:
Colossians 2:13 says that before you knew Christ, you were spiritually dead because of your trespasses and because your sinful nature was not set apart for God. But God made you alive together with Christ and forgave all your trespasses. In this verse, "made you alive" describes the new life God gives through Christ.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Colossae, many of whom did not come from a Jewish background. He reminds them of what God has already done for them in Christ, so that they will not be misled by teachings that insisted on extra rituals and rules as if these were required for salvation. The verses that follow speak of a record of debt against them that God set aside by nailing it to the cross.

For today: if you trust in Christ, you do not have to earn forgiveness through religious effort or live weighed down by guilt that has already been forgiven. You can start each day thankful, knowing that God has given you new life.
exp.2:17:
Paul asks wives to submit to their husbands. Submitting means willingly placing oneself under the husband's leadership, and the phrase "as is fitting in the Lord" indicates that this should be done as part of living for Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae, probably while he is in prison. After speaking of a life filled with the word of Christ, he gives instructions for the home: to wives, husbands, and children. In the ancient world this was common, but Paul places it "in the Lord" and also requires love and tenderness from husbands. Christians understand the scope of this submission in different ways.

For today: in marriage, let both seek to honor Christ with respect, dialogue, and love. Before a disagreement, pray together and ask: "How can we please the Lord in this?"
exp.1:6:
This verse uses the picture of a tree and of a house. To be "rooted" means to have deep roots in Christ. To be "built up" means that life keeps being built on him, like a house on a good foundation. To be "established in the faith" means standing firm in what was believed, just as it was taught. To be "overflowing with thankfulness" means giving thanks, that is, living in a grateful way.

Paul writes to the believers in Colossae, although he is far away from them. He rejoices to see their good order and their firmness. He asks them to keep living in Christ as they first received him. He also warns them not to be deceived by human teachings that draw them away from Christ.

For today: just as a tree grows when it has good roots, our faith grows when we return to Christ each day. A simple practice is to read a little of the Bible and end by giving thanks for something specific.
exp.0:12:
Paul says that God the Father has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his beloved Son. "Dominion" means rule or authority. "Darkness" stands for evil, sin, and not knowing God. "Brought us into" means that God moved us from one realm to another, like someone who crosses from one country into another.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, a city he had not visited personally, as the text makes clear. He thanks them for their faith and prays for them. Here he reminds them of what God has already done for them. Then, in the verses that follow, he presents Christ as the one who gives us redemption and forgiveness.

For today: if God has already brought you into his kingdom, you do not have to live as a slave to guilt or old habits. Today you can remember who you are in Christ and ask him for help to live as a citizen of his kingdom.
exp.1:20:
This verse repeats the rules that some people wanted to impose on believers: "Do not handle," "do not taste," "do not touch!" "Handle" here means to grab or take hold of with the hands, and "taste" means to try by mouth. Each prohibition is stricter than the one before, with the last one, "do not touch," sounding the most severe.

Paul writes to the Colossians, who were facing teachers who mixed human rules, rituals, and a harsh religiosity. Paul quotes their rules, probably with some irony, to ask why those who died with Christ would go back to submitting to them. It is not known exactly what all those rules were, but he calls them "the doctrines of men."

Today we can ask ourselves whether we measure our faith by a list of prohibitions. Rules may appear to be wisdom, but they do not change the heart. Our life grows by remaining united to Christ, the Head.
exp.2:10:
In the new life with Christ, the divisions that separate people fall away. "Greek" and "Jew" name groups of different origin, and "circumcised" and "uncircumcised" refer to those who bore the Jewish mark and those who did not. A "barbarian" was someone who did not speak Greek, and the Scythians were seen as a very savage people. A "slave" was someone owned by another person. The central point is that Christ is all and is in all.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae from prison. He reminds them that they have already put off the old way of living and put on the new. Therefore no one is worth more because of their origin, culture, or social position.

For today: before judging someone by their country, their money, or their accent, remember that Christ is also in that person. Treat someone different from you with respect and kindness today.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that the peace that comes from Christ should "rule" in our hearts, meaning it should be the one that decides and guides us when there is tension or doubt. That peace is something we were called to as members of one body, the church. It ends with an invitation: "And be thankful."

The writer is the apostle Paul, addressing the believers in Colossae. He has just asked them for patience, forgiveness, and love toward one another, as Christ forgave them. That is why peace is not only a personal feeling but something that unites the community. Afterward, Paul speaks of the word of Christ, the singing, and gratitude.

For today: before you respond in a family disagreement or at church, pause and pray. Ask yourself which decision keeps peace and forgiveness alive. Then thank God for something concrete about that person.
exp.2:18:
Husbands are told to love their wives and not to be harsh with them. The word "harsh" here means being rough, hard, or difficult to deal with. Other versions say "do not be harsh" or "do not be bitter toward them."

Paul is writing to the believers in Colossae and giving instructions for life at home. Before this verse he speaks to wives, and after it he speaks to children and to fathers. The whole passage is under the idea of doing everything "in the name of the Lord Jesus." In his time, asking a husband for love and tenderness was a call to live with the character of Christ, not only with authority.

For today: watch your manner of speaking and reacting at home. If you become irritated, pause, answer with calm, and look for a concrete way to serve or encourage your wife today.
exp.0:23:
Paul says he rejoices in his sufferings, because he endures them for the good of the believers. He says that in his own body he fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions on behalf of the church, which is his body. "Rejoice" here means being glad.

Paul writes from prison to the Colossians, and he presents himself as a minister of the gospel. His suffering is part of his service. The phrase "what is lacking" is understood in several ways. Many believers do not take it to mean something incomplete in Christ's saving work, but rather the sufferings his people share when they carry the gospel.

For today: when serving others costs you effort or discomfort, do not think it is wasted time. Ask God to give you joy, and remember that, united with Christ, your devotion has meaning.
exp.1:0:
Paul tells the Christians of Colossae how deeply he cares for them. The word "struggling" describes intense care and effort on their behalf. His concern reaches the believers at Laodicea and all who have never met him face to face.

Paul probably wrote this letter from prison. Many understand that he did not found the church at Colossae; another man worked there, such as Epaphras. Even so, Paul cares for them as a pastor, because he wants them to stand firm, united in love and rooted in Christ, in the face of deceptive teachings.

For today: we can love and pray for brothers and sisters we do not know well, such as missionaries, believers who are persecuted, or distant churches. Today, name someone like this before God and ask that their heart be strengthened.
exp.2:24:
This verse says that whoever does wrong to others will receive the consequences of what they did. "Wrong" here means injustice, a harm done to someone, not only an insult. "Favoritism" means that God does not treat some people better than others because of their position or importance.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae and, just before this, speaks to servants, or slaves, urging them to work wholeheartedly, as for the Lord. This verse serves as a general warning: no one escapes the justice of God, neither the servant nor the master (in 4:1 Paul addresses masters). Some think it refers to the servant who does wrong; others believe it includes anyone who mistreats another. The text allows both readings.

For today: treat everyone with justice and honesty, whether your boss, an employee, or a stranger, remembering that God sees everything and shows no favoritism.
exp.1:15:
Paul tells the believers that no one should criticize them or make them feel guilty about what they eat or drink, or about how they keep the feasts, the New Moon, or the Sabbath. "Judge you" here means "condemn you" or "criticize you." A New Moon was a celebration held at the start of each month.

Paul writes to the Christians in Colossae, who were under pressure from teachers who mixed Jewish rules with strange spiritual practices. Earlier in the letter he said that Christ canceled the debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross. For that reason, these rules are not the basis for being right with God. The verses that follow call them a "shadow," while the "body," or reality, is Christ. Some debate how this applies to the Sabbath, but the central point is that no one should impose these things as a requirement for salvation.

Today, let us not measure the faith of others by their customs, nor let others measure us that way. Let us seek Christ first and treat with love those who think differently.
exp.3:6:
Paul says that Tychicus will tell them all the news about his situation. The word "state" in the older text has nothing to do with commerce or trade; it refers to what is happening to Paul, his circumstances and affairs. Tychicus is described as a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and he closes with greetings and personal news. Instead of writing out all the details himself, he sends Tychicus, a trusted coworker, to report in person and to encourage the Colossians. Paul does not present himself as superior but honors Tychicus as a fellow servant with equal standing in the work.

For today: value those who serve you faithfully, even when they are quiet about it, and share your life with other believers. Faith grows when we stay close, keep one another informed with care, and encourage each other.
exp.2:8:
Colossians 3:9 says that believers should not lie to one another. The reason is that they have already taken off the old self, the old way of living apart from God, along with its practices. The verse uses the word "lie," and it also speaks of taking off the old self, so both ideas come straight from the text. The "practices" are simply the actions and habits that made up that old way of life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae. He reminds them that before, they lived in anger, malice, and harmful speech. Now, united to Christ, they are new people who are being renewed. That is why truth must shape their relationships, regardless of their background or social position.

Today, let us think about a small lie we tend to tell, such as an excuse, an exaggeration, or a half-truth. Today, with God's help, let us decide to speak with honesty and kindness, especially with our family, our church, and our coworkers.
exp.3:15:
Paul asks that the letter to the Colossians, once it has been read among you, also be read in the church of the Laodiceans. He also asks you to read the letter that comes from Laodicea. The phrases "make sure that it is also read" and "that you in turn read" are easy to understand today: they mean "make sure this letter is read there too" and "that you read the letter from Laodicea yourselves."

Paul writes from prison, as he says at the end of the letter. Colossae and Laodicea were neighboring cities, and letters were read aloud to the whole congregation. We do not know for certain which letter the one "from Laodicea" was: some think it was a letter of Paul that has been lost, while others think it is the letter we now call Ephesians. Scholars do not agree.

Today we can learn from this practice: God's Word is not only for my church or for me alone. Let us share what we learn from the Bible with other believers, and stay open to learning from what God has taught other communities.
exp.0:22:
The explanation says that the reconciliation Christ gave us is to be lived out with steadfastness. "If indeed" means "but if," that is, on the condition that they keep going this way. "Established and firm" means well founded, like a house built on rock, stable and not easily shaken. "Not moved from the hope of the gospel" means not allowing oneself to be drawn away from it. The hope of the gospel is the good news you have heard. "Proclaimed to every creature under heaven" shows that the message is for everyone. Paul describes himself as a servant of that gospel.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae from prison, as the letter itself indicates. He reminds them of what Christ has done for them and encourages them not to turn aside, since there were teachings that could draw them away from simple faith in Christ.

Today: when doubts arise or ideas that seem more appealing come along, return to the basics. Read the Gospels, pray, and gather with other believers, so that your faith has deep roots and does not get blown about by every wind.
exp.3:4:
Paul asks the believers to act wisely toward outsiders, meaning people who are not Christians. "Redeeming the time" means making the most of every opportunity, like someone who buys something valuable and does not let it slip away.

Paul writes this letter from prison. He has just asked for prayer that God would open a door for him so he can proclaim the gospel clearly. Now he reminds the Colossians that they too are witnesses of Christ. Their daily conduct speaks, so he tells them their words should be gracious and well considered.

Today we can ask ourselves: how does someone who does not believe see me? A simple application is to treat coworkers and neighbors with respect and patience, and to stay alert for a conversation where we can offer a word of hope, without pressuring anyone.
exp.3:7:
Paul sent Tychicus to the Colossians for two reasons: so that they would know how Paul and his companions were doing, and so that their hearts would be encouraged. In this verse, "know about us" means knowing how Paul and his companions were getting along, and "encourage your hearts" means cheering them up and strengthening them.

Paul writes from prison to the church in Colossae. He could not visit them himself, so he sent Tychicus, whom he calls a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant. Onesimus went with him, and together they would bring news and encouragement. This shows that Paul cared for the churches closely and worked through the help of others.

For today: do not underestimate the value of a visit, a phone call, or a sincere message. Ask yourself whom you could encourage this week, and do it with kind and true words, as Paul asked in the previous verse.
exp.1:13:
He says that God canceled the debt that stood against us. Canceling a debt means wiping the record clean, so that what was owed no longer counts against anyone. The debt was a written record of what we owed, so removing it means the debt is gone. The "decrees that stood against us" refers to written rules or requirements, and people understand them in different ways: some think of the law of Moses, others of our debt of sin. God took the debt out of the way and nailed it to the cross of Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, most of whom were not Jewish. He has just said that God forgave them and gave them life with Christ. Then he warns them that no one should judge them over food, festivals, or sabbaths. He wants them to rest in what Christ has already done.

If you live with guilt over your past, remember that in Christ the debt has been canceled. You no longer have to earn forgiveness through religious effort. Rest in his grace and serve him with gratitude.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that Epaphras, the same man who taught you the gospel, told Paul about the love you had. "Informed" means "told" or "reported." "In the Spirit" means that this love did not come only from human effort, but was the work of the Holy Spirit in you.

Paul writes this letter together with Timothy to a church he did not found and had not personally visited. Epaphras had preached to them and then brought news to Paul. Before correcting mistaken ideas, Paul acknowledges the good that was among them and shows that he is thankful and close to them.

For today: when you see genuine love in other believers, tell them. A sincere word of encouragement strengthens people. And ask the Spirit to grow in you a love that does not depend only on your own strength.
exp.2:16:
Whatever you do, whether in what you say or in what you do, should be done in the name of the Lord Jesus. This means acting as someone who belongs to him and represents him. At the same time, you give thanks to God the Father through Him.

The letter was written by the apostle Paul to the Christians in Colossae. Earlier in the letter he speaks of God's peace, thankfulness, and the word of Christ living richly in the heart. Afterward he gives instructions for daily life at home. In this way, the verse joins both parts together: faith is lived out in everyday life.

For today: before you speak, answer a message, or begin your work, ask yourself, "Does this reflect Jesus?" Then thank God for that moment, even if it is a simple one.
exp.2:19:
It says that children should obey their parents in everything, because that pleases God. The phrase "in everything" means in every area of daily life, though the New Testament also teaches that our final loyalty belongs to God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae. After speaking about the new life in Christ, he gives instructions for the home: wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants. It is notable that he teaches children as responsible members of the community of faith. Next he asks fathers not to provoke their children to anger.

For today: if you are a son or daughter, practice obedience as a way of honoring God, with respect and a good attitude. If you are already an adult, you can honor your parents by listening to them, caring for them, and speaking to them with affection.
exp.0:20:
The explanation says that the Christians of Colossae, before, were far from God and hostile to him in their minds, because their thoughts and their evil deeds set them against him. The word "alienated" means "far away from God" and refers to being separated from him. Now God has reconciled them, that is, he has restored peace and friendship with them.

Paul writes this letter to a church that he himself had not founded. He speaks first of the greatness of Christ, and through his cross God makes peace. Paul reminds them of what they were and of what God did, so that they stay firm in the gospel and are not led away by other teachings.

Today, if you feel far from God because of your mistakes, remember that reconciliation is a gift that he has already offered in Christ. Come near with confidence, and live thankfully, letting that peace change your thoughts and your decisions.
exp.2:9:
It says that believers have already put on a new life, the way someone changes clothes. The verb here can also be rendered "dress yourselves" or "clothe yourselves." The new life is being renewed through knowledge, that is, by coming to know God better, and each day it looks more and more like the image of its Creator.

Paul writes to the church in Colossae. He asks them to set aside anger, malice, filthy speech and lying, because they have already taken off the old self, that is, their former way of living. In the verses that follow he says that in Christ there are no differences between people, and that everyone should clothe themselves with compassion and humility.

For today: when a surge of anger or the pull to lie comes over you, remember who you are in Christ. Pause, pray, and choose a gentle response, the way someone chooses what clothes to put on.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that the gospel, which is mentioned in the previous verse, has come to the Colossians. And not only to them: it is bearing fruit and growing all over the world, just as it has been doing among them. "Bearing fruit" means that it produces real change, that is, changed lives. This began when they heard the gospel and truly understood the grace of God, his love and undeserved favor.

Paul writes this letter, together with Timothy, to a church he did not found. Epaphras had taught them the gospel. Paul thanks God for their faith and love, and reminds them that the message they received is the same, true and powerful, that is preached in other places.

For today: the gospel is not only heard, it also bears fruit. Ask yourself what changes it is producing in the way you love, forgive, and live. Keep growing in the grace of God every day.
exp.2:21:
Slaves were to obey their earthly masters in everything. "Earthly masters" means the human owners of this world. Working hard only when someone is watching, in order to look good before people, is what the verse calls merely pleasing them while they are watching. Instead, they should serve with sincerity of heart, meaning wholehearted honesty, and with reverence for the Lord.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae, and in this passage he gives instructions to different members of the household. Slavery was common in the Roman world at that time. Paul neither approves of nor condemns it here; he speaks to believers who lived within that reality and shows them how to live out their faith. Some scholars think this planted ideas that later would challenge that system.

For today: work honestly even when no one is watching you, knowing that God does see. Do your work with sincerity, as an act of respect toward Him.
exp.2:15:
Let the message of Christ settle deeply and richly into your life, bringing wisdom in every area. Let it shape how you teach and encourage one another, and let it come out in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing with gratitude in your hearts to God.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, probably from prison, to strengthen them in Christ. Just before, he spoke of the love and peace that unite the church. This verse shows how that unity is lived out: through God's word and shared worship. He then goes on to speak of doing everything in the name of Jesus.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading the Bible, and share with someone, in person or by message, a verse or a song that has encouraged you.
exp.1:17:
Paul warns that no one should take away your "reward," meaning the blessing that comes from following Christ. He speaks of someone who delights in false humility and in the worship of angels. That person pushes into speculation about what he claims to have seen, and he is puffed up with pride by an unspiritual mind. "False humility" means appearing to be humble when one is not, and "without basis" means with no real foundation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Colossae, who were under pressure from teachings that mixed rules, rituals, and spiritual experiences. Scholars debate exactly which group this was. Paul insists that all of that is a shadow and that the reality is found in Christ, the Head.

Today, be wary of anyone who boasts of special experiences or an outward show of humility and draws you away from Christ. Examine every teaching in the light of Jesus, not by the impression it makes.
exp.3:13:
Paul sends greetings from two companions who were with him: Luke, whom he calls "the beloved physician," and Demas. The phrase "send you greetings" means that they pass along their good wishes to you. Paul uses an affectionate description for Luke and adds no comment about Demas.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Colossae, probably while he is in prison. At the end he mentions several co-workers whom the Colossians knew or had heard named. Many believe this Luke is the author of the Gospel that bears his name, although the letter does not say so directly. Later, in other letters, Paul speaks of Demas with sadness (2 Timothy 4:10).

For today: value and express affection toward those who serve alongside you, even in simple tasks. A sincere greeting or a word of appreciation strengthens the faith of others. And remember that persevering matters more than starting well.
exp.1:8:
It says that in Jesus Christ all the fullness of God dwells, that is, everything God is, and that this became real in a human body. "Deity" refers to the nature of God. "In bodily form" points to that fullness being shown in a body; some understand it as referring to Jesus in the flesh, and others also see it as a present and visible reality in Christ.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Colosse to protect them from deceptive teachings, which wanted to add other things to Christ. Paul responds by showing that Christ is already complete and sufficient. The exact details of that error in Colosse are debated among scholars.

If Christ has all the fullness of God, you do not need to look elsewhere for whatever you lack in order to be right with God. When you feel confused by new ideas or spiritual pressures, return to Jesus and trust that in him you already have what is essential.
exp.1:2:
In Christ are kept all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The word "hidden" does not mean they are secret forever. It means they are kept safe like a valuable treasure, waiting for someone to seek them in Him.

Paul writes from prison to Christians in Colossae and Laodicea, most of whom he had never met in person. He was worried that someone would deceive them with arguments that sounded very intelligent. So he reminds them that they do not need to look for true wisdom anywhere else, because it is already found in Christ.

For today: when you feel confused by so many opinions, return to Jesus. Read the Gospels calmly and ask God for understanding before making important decisions.
exp.1:9:
The explanation says that believers have been made complete, that is, whole and full, because they are united with Christ. Nothing essential is lacking for them to stand right with God. Christ is also the one who rules over every ruler and authority. These words refer to spiritual powers and authorities. Some think this also includes human authorities, but the text does not spell that out.

Paul writes to the church in Colossae, which was in danger of being deceived by philosophies and human traditions. Those teachings made it seem as though Christ was not enough. That is why Paul reminds them that in Christ dwells the whole fullness of God, and that whoever has him no longer needs additions.

For today: when you feel you must add rituals, methods, or new ideas to be accepted by God, remember that in Christ you are already complete. Rest in him and live thankfully.
exp.2:23:
Verse 24 says that believers can work with peace of mind, knowing that God himself will give them an inheritance as their reward. The phrase about receiving the inheritance is best read as a reward that comes as part of what God gives his children. And where the earlier wording speaks of believers serving, the sense is that the one they serve is the Lord Christ.

Paul is writing to the church in Colossae. He addresses the slaves, who lived under human masters and had no rights. He reminds them that their work, even in such a hard situation, can be done for the Lord. This does not approve of slavery; it only shows how to live with dignity and faith within it. The following verse adds that God judges with justice, without favoritism.

Today, if your work is heavy or no one recognizes it, you can do it with honesty and good spirit, as for the Lord. His approval is worth more than that of any boss.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that whatever we do, we should work at it with our whole being, as something done for the Lord and not just to please people. To work "with your whole being" means giving it real effort and sincerity, with all your heart. "Whatever" simply means any task at all.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Colosse. Earlier he spoke to parents and children, and then to the servants (slaves) of that time. He teaches them to work with sincerity, not only when the master is watching. Then he promises that the Lord himself will reward them, because in the end it is Christ whom they serve.

Today, this applies to your work, your studies, or your household chores. Do them with honesty and effort, even when no one is watching or applauding. Before you begin, you can say a short prayer such as: "Lord, I do this for you."
exp.1:3:
Paul says he is writing what came before so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric. He means well-crafted, convincing speeches that sound wise but lead people into error. The phrase "deceive you" means "confuse you or lead you astray." The point is that something can sound very good and still not be true.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, whom he probably did not know personally. He speaks to them about Christ, in whom are "all the treasures of wisdom." His concern is that some were teaching ideas that drew people away from Christ. The Bible does not spell out here exactly what those ideas were, and scholars debate their origin. Paul wants their faith to remain firm.

Today, before accepting a teaching that sounds very convincing, ask yourself: does it bring me closer to Christ, and does it agree with what the Scriptures say? Studying the Bible with other believers helps us avoid being carried away merely by the attractiveness of a speech.
exp.2:0:
Since you have been raised with Christ, set your heart and your efforts on "the things above." There Christ is seated at the right hand of God, that is, in the place of honor and authority.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Colossae. He writes to remind them that, through faith, their lives are united with Christ in his death and his resurrection. For this reason he encourages them to live in line with that new identity and not to be carried away by teachings that were pulling them away from Christ.

For today: before you begin your day, take a few minutes to pray and read the Bible, and ask God to help you choose according to the values of Christ: to be honest, patient, and generous, even when no one sees you or applauds you.
exp.3:1:
They are told to keep devoting themselves to prayer without giving up. "Devote yourselves" means to commit firmly and not grow tired. "Being watchful" means staying awake and attentive while praying, not doing it out of habit. "Thankful" refers to giving thanks to God.

Paul writes this letter from prison, as the following verses show. Earlier he gave instructions about life in the home, including to masters and servants. Here he sums everything up with a call to prayer. Right after this he asks them to pray for him and his companions, so that God will open doors and they can proclaim Christ clearly.

Today we can choose a fixed time of day to pray, and begin or end by giving thanks for something specific. In this way prayer becomes an attentive and grateful habit, not just a list of requests.
exp.3:16:
Paul asks the Colossians to pass a message on to Archippus: that he should pay close attention to the service he received from the Lord and carry it through to completion. The word "ministry" in the verse means the service or work entrusted to someone, and "See to it that you complete" means "take care to finish it well."

Paul writes this letter from prison, near the end, while he sends greetings. We do not know for certain what Archippus's ministry was. It is thought that he lived in Colossae or nearby, and in Philemon 2 Paul calls him a fellow soldier. Some believe he was a son or relative of Philemon, but that is not certain.

For today: God gives each believer a service, whether great or small. Ask yourself what the Lord has entrusted to you and what concrete step you can take this week to keep moving forward faithfully, without leaving it half done.
exp.0:4:
Paul says that he gives thanks to God for the faith and love of the Colossians, which come from the hope stored up for them in heaven. The phrase "stored up for you" means that this hope is kept safe and reserved for them. They first heard about it when they heard the word of truth, the gospel, that is, the message of Jesus, which does not deceive.

Paul is writing to a church he did not found. Epaphras had taught them, and Paul rejoices at what he has heard about them. Many understand that faith and love grow out of this sure hope. Paul wants to encourage them and also to prepare them to remain steadfast in the true gospel.

Today, when life feels uncertain or weary, remember that your hope in Christ does not depend on your circumstances, because God keeps it. That assurance can help you go on believing and loving others with patience.
exp.2:6:
In these practices, the believers in Colossae also once lived. The verse names sexual immorality, impurity, evil desires, and greed. The word "walk" in the verse means that they conducted their lives in these ways, and "when you lived among them" points to their life before they came to know Christ. The phrase "you also used to walk in these ways" shows that this was not an occasional lapse, but their regular way of life.

Paul writes this letter, and tradition says he wrote it while in prison, to a church that he himself had not founded. After warning about God's judgment against rebellion, he reminds them of their past. He does not do this to shame them, but to show them the contrast: what once defined them no longer belongs to them, because now they belong to Christ.

Remembering where God rescued us keeps us humble and grateful. It helps us not to judge harshly those who still live this way, and it encourages us to leave behind old habits, trusting that Christ gives us a new life.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that God has reconciled us to himself through the death of Jesus, who took on a real physical body. The purpose is to present us before him as holy (set apart for God), blameless (free from guilt), and without blemish (with nothing for anyone to find fault with in us).

Paul is writing to the Christians in Colossae. He reminds them that they were once far from God, and that now Christ has reconciled them. He speaks this way to affirm that Jesus is enough, and to encourage them to remain firm in the faith of the gospel, without letting themselves be led away by other teachings.

For today: if you feel unworthy or carry guilt from your past, remember that your cleansing does not depend on your efforts, but on what Christ has already done. Rest in his forgiveness and live gratefully, staying firm in him.
exp.3:3:
This verse is part of Paul's request: that they pray for him to be able to make the mystery of Christ clear. "Declare it clearly" means to make something plain so that it can be understood. "As I should" means: in the right and fitting way, as he ought to do.

Paul writes this letter from prison. He asks the Colossians to pray steadily and with thanksgiving, not that he be released, but that God would open doors for him to proclaim the gospel. Even in chains, his main concern is to explain the message of Christ well. Then he asks them to speak as well, with wisdom and grace.

For today: before you speak about your faith, ask God for clarity and good manner. And pray for those who share the gospel, that they do it with truth, simplicity and love.
exp.3:0:
Paul tells masters to deal with those who work under them in ways that are right and fair. The people in view here are slaves or workers who are under the authority of their masters. The reason he gives is that masters also have a Master in heaven, and they too will answer to Him.

The apostle Paul writes this letter while he is in prison. Earlier in the letter he spoke to wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants. Now he addresses masters. Slavery was common in the ancient world, and Paul does not present it as an ideal, but he limits the potential for abuse by reminding everyone that they are accountable to God.

For today: if you have authority over others, such as a boss, a teacher, or a parent, treat people justly, pay what is owed, and respect their dignity, remembering that you too will answer to God.
exp.1:1:
Paul hopes that the hearts of the believers will be encouraged and strengthened, that they will be joined together in love, and that they will have the full riches of complete understanding. To be encouraged means to be lifted up and strengthened. Complete means nothing is missing. All of this serves the goal of knowing the mystery of God, which is Christ.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians of Colossae. He tells them that he struggles in prayer and with concern for them, for the believers in Laodicea, and for others who never knew him personally. According to the following verse, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found in Christ, and Paul wants to protect them from those who were deceiving them with persuasive but false words.

For today: do not seek security only in new ideas or convincing speeches. Grow in the knowledge of Christ through the Bible and prayer, and do it together with others, loving and supporting your brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that Jesus is the Creator of all things. Everything that exists, whether we can see it or not, was created in him, through him, and for him. The words "thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities" are names for powers, perhaps spiritual ones, and some think they may also include human rulers. None of them stands above Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae. There were teachings that placed Jesus as just one more among other spiritual powers. Paul answers by showing that Christ is the image of the invisible God, that he created all things, and that he also redeemed us with his blood.

For today: if all things were created for Jesus, then your life is too. Today, before deciding something, ask him: "Lord, how can I live this for you?" And do not fear anything, because he is above all.
exp.1:19:
If we have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, then it makes no sense to keep living as though we still belonged to that system. To "submit to its regulations" means putting ourselves under rules that others impose. Paul asks: why would you do that?

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, who were being pressured by teachers who demanded rituals, prohibitions, and a certain worship of angels. Some scholars think these teachers mixed Jewish and philosophical ideas, though this cannot be known with certainty. Paul reminds them that their union with Christ, the Head, is enough for them.

For today: do not measure your life with God by lists of "do not do this" created by people. Cultivate your closeness to Christ, and let his love and his Word shape your conduct from the heart.
exp.0:3:
Paul says that he has heard about the faith the Colossians have in Christ Jesus and about their love for all the saints. "Saints" does not refer to perfect people, but to all who belong to God through Christ. The phrase "because we have heard" means that Paul received good news about them.

Paul writes this letter with Timothy to a church in Colossae. According to the text, Paul did not know them in person, and he learned about them from others. He begins by giving thanks to God and praying for them. Here he highlights two signs of a healthy Christian life: faith in Christ and love toward other believers.
