Afterward he mentions the hope that sustains them.

For today: true faith shows itself in concrete love. Think of a brother or sister in your church and today serve them, call them, or pray for them. In this way your trust in Christ becomes visible.
exp.1:22:
These rules, such as "do not handle, do not taste, do not touch," may look wise. They seem to call for a worship you choose yourself, a humility that is not real, and a harsh treatment of the body. Yet they do not actually hold back the desires of the flesh, meaning the selfish pull within a human being.

Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, warning them against teachers who mixed religious practices, rules of abstinence, and an apparent humility. He insists that Christ is enough and that rules made up by people do not change the heart. Scholars debate exactly who those teachers were, but the central message is clear.

Today, do not trust that more rules or sacrifices will make you a better person. Seek to have Christ change your heart, and let love and gratitude toward Him guide the way you live.
exp.0:11:
He says we give thanks to the Father because he has qualified us to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. "Inheritance" here does not mean luck or chance, but a portion that is received. The "saints" are those who belong to God, and "in the light" speaks of living in God's sphere, not in darkness.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae while he is in prison. He tells them what he asks for them: that they live in a way worthy of the Lord. Here he adds that gratitude sustains that life. The verses that follow explain that God rescued us from darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his Son, where there is forgiveness.

For today: you do not have to earn your place with God, because he has already qualified you. Today, before you worry about what you lack, give thanks for what he has already given you in Christ.
exp.2:12:
It says we should bear with one another patiently and forgive each other when someone has a complaint against another. "Bear with" means putting up with others and having patience with them. A "complaint" is a grievance or an offense. The model is Christ: just as he forgave us, we too must forgive.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Colossae. He has just said that in Christ the divisions between peoples and social classes are erased. So he asks them to live as God's chosen people, clothed in mercy, humility and gentleness. Forgiveness is the practical way of living out that unity, and love binds it all together.

For today: think of someone who has bothered or offended you. Before responding in anger, remember how much Christ has forgiven you. Take one concrete step: pray for that person, speak to them calmly, or let go of the resentment.

sum.2: Paul teaches that since believers have been raised with Christ, they should set their minds on the things above and leave behind sin, such as sexual immorality, greed, anger, and lying. They should clothe themselves with compassion, humility, forgiveness, and love, letting the peace and the word of Christ guide their lives. He also gives instructions to husbands, children, parents, and servants, so that they do everything for the Lord.
sum.0: Paul gives thanks to God for the faith, love, and hope of the believers in Colossae, and he prays that they will grow in wisdom and bear fruit. He teaches that Jesus is the image of the invisible God, the Creator and the head of the church, and that through his cross he reconciles us to God. Paul serves the church and proclaims Christ, the hope of glory.
sum.3: Paul encourages believers to pray steadily and with thankfulness, to treat their servants fairly, and to live wisely and speak graciously to those who do not believe. He then sends greetings from his companions, including Tychicus, Onesimus, Mark, Epaphras, and Luke, asks that the letter also be read in Laodicea, and urges Archippus to carry out the ministry he has received.
sum.1: Paul shows how deeply he cares about the believers in Colossae and Laodicea, and he warns them not to be taken in by human philosophies. He reminds them that all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, that through Him they were forgiven and raised to new life, and that they no longer need to submit to religious rules made by people.
